opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is not to copy what your role models did, but to understand why they did it. When I look at people I admire, whether they're researchers, engineers, or founders, it's tempting to just look at the outcome. You see the famous paper, the successful company, the elegant system, and you think, "I want that." But the outcome is usually the least transferable part. Their circumstances, their timing, their luck: none of that you can reproduce.

What you *can* learn is how they think. How do they choose problems? What do they say no to? How do they handle the period when nobody believes in what they're doing? I've found that if you read carefully, or if you're lucky enough to talk with them directly, the decision-making process is much more valuable than the achievement itself.

Another thing I try to keep in mind is that role models are people, not gods. Everyone has weaknesses, and everyone made mistakes along the way. If you idealize someone too much, you either feel hopeless because the gap seems impossible, or you start imitating their flaws along with their strengths. So I try to take specific pieces: maybe one person's taste in research problems, another person's work ethic, another person's way of communicating with a team. Then I combine them into something that fits me.

And finally, at some point you have to stop looking outward. Role models are very useful early on, when you don't yet know what's possible. But eventually you need to develop your own judgment, your own taste, and be willing to go in a direction nobody has gone before. In a way, the best thing you can learn from great people is the courage to not follow anyone, including them.

r001.rationale: The response says to study how admired people think and make decisions, because that process is more transferable than their achievements; it presents this as a way to learn and develop one’s own judgment.

r002.rationale: The response encourages developing independent judgment and choosing one’s own direction, but does not say that a person’s past identity need not constrain who they can become.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about role models a little differently than most people, because I try not to have just one. When you pick a single person and say "I want to be them," you end up copying things that don't actually fit you, including their flaws. What I do instead is look at a lot of people and borrow one specific thing from each.

For example, from some of the engineers I worked with at MIT, I learned to care about the small details, like how clean a piece of code is or how carefully a benchmark is set up. From some of the founders I admire, I learned the opposite skill, which is to ignore a hundred details and focus on the one decision that actually matters this month. Those two things almost contradict each other, and that's the point. No single person has both, so you have to assemble your own version.

The second thing is that I try to learn from how they think, not just what they did. When I read about someone like Jim Keller or Jeff Dean, the interesting part isn't the chip or the system they built. It's the questions they asked at the beginning, when nothing was obvious yet. If you can reconstruct that reasoning, you can apply it to a completely different problem. If you only copy the output, you're just a few years behind.

And the last piece, honestly, is that a lot of my role models are not famous. Some are students I've mentored who are much better than I am at something specific, like writing or being patient with users. I think if you only look up, you miss half of what's there to learn. So I try to stay curious about everyone around me and keep a running list of what each person does better than me. That list is probably the most useful document I own.

r001.rationale: The response describes borrowing specific skills and reconstructing role models’ reasoning, but it does not present examining why they succeeded as a way to improve oneself.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that a person’s past need not constrain who they can become.

astra-6.text:
I think the most useful thing is to understand how they think, rather than just copy what they do. When someone is very successful, you see the outcome, but you don’t necessarily see the decisions, mistakes, and constraints that led them there. I try to ask: What did they know at the time? Why did they choose that direction? And which parts of that reasoning apply to my situation?

You can also learn different things from different people. You don’t have to find one person and follow everything they do. Ultimately, learning from role models should help you develop your own judgment.

r001.rationale: The candidate says to examine successful role models’ decisions and reasoning, then apply relevant lessons to develop one’s own judgment.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses developing independent judgment but does not say that a person’s past need not constrain who they can become.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most useful thing is to understand how your role models think, rather than simply copying what they do. Their choices come from a particular context, and your situation may be different. So I try to ask: What questions are they asking? How do they decide what is worth working on? How do they respond when something doesn’t work?

You can learn different things from different people. You don’t have to follow one person in every dimension. Ultimately, learning from role models should help you develop your own judgment.
